docs.title: LadderOps documentation
docs.text: LadderOps is a records management system for fire and EMS departments. It replaces the paperwork side of running a department: the incident record that has to go to NERIS, the roster, the apparatus list, and the checks and inspections your crews already do on paper.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
If you are setting up a department for the first time, read Your first week. It covers the checklist that has to be finished before your first call can be reported, and what each item is for.

If you are already set up and want to know how a call gets from the tones dropping to a submitted NERIS record, read Reporting a call.

docs.title: What is in this guide
docs.text:
The guide is written for the person doing the job, not for an administrator of the software. It names buttons the way the screen names them and it says what happens when you press them.

Every page inside LadderOps also has a Help button in the bottom right corner that shows the part of this guide written about that page, so you rarely need to come here to look something up mid-call.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text: The API reference documents every endpoint, generated from the running application, so it cannot describe an API we are not shipping.

docs.title: Something wrong or missing?
docs.text: Inside the app, the Help button has a Report a problem tab that sends us what you were doing along with your message. That is the fastest way to get something fixed.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Every endpoint LadderOps serves, generated from the running application and checked against it by CI, so this cannot drift from what we are shipping.

Authentication is a bearer token. Paths carry no version prefix.

docs.title: Recording mutual and automatic aid
docs.text: Every call where another department helped you, or you helped them, has to name that department on the NERIS record. LadderOps keeps a list of the departments you work with so you pick from it on the incident form instead of typing a NERIS ID each time.

docs.title: Set up your partners once
docs.text:
Open Aid Agreements and choose Add nearby departments. LadderOps reads the NERIS directory for your county and lists every registered department, with the ones you already have marked. Untick any you do not run aid with, choose the agreement type (most rural partners are mutual aid), and add the rest in one step.

To find a department in another county, change the NERIS ID prefix to that county, or search by name.

Each partner can be edited later. Change the agreement type, add notes, or mark a partner inactive when an agreement ends. An inactive partner disappears from the incident picker but stays on the incidents where it was already recorded, so past reports do not change.

docs.title: On the incident
docs.text:
In the incident's aid section, pick the partner from the list, say whether aid was given or received, and choose the aid type. The partner's NERIS ID comes along automatically. If a department that is not on your list helped, you can still type its name and NERIS ID for that one call.

Fire departments are the only partners NERIS lets you record under an agreement. Other agencies on scene, such as EMS, law enforcement, or utilities, are recorded separately as non-fire agencies on the same section.

docs.title: If NERIS is not connected yet
docs.text: Adding nearby departments needs your department's NERIS credentials, because the directory is read through them. Until NERIS is connected, add partners by hand from the same page.

docs.title: Apparatus and the daily check
docs.text: Your apparatus list is the backbone of most of what LadderOps does. Incidents are staffed from it, checks are run against it, and equipment hangs off it. It is worth getting right once.

docs.title: Adding your apparatus
docs.text:
Open Apparatus & Equipment from the menu, then Apparatus. Choose New Apparatus.

Three things are required and the form will not save without them:

  • Call sign, the name your crews actually say on the radio. Engine 1, Tanker 2, Brush 1.
  • Organization, which department the vehicle belongs to. Even if you only have one, you have to pick it.
  • Apparatus type, the NERIS category. Engine, tanker, ambulance, and so on.

Everything else, including make, model, year, station, and how many the vehicle seats, can be filled in later. Staffing capacity is worth setting early because the incident form uses it.

If your apparatus already exist in a spreadsheet, use Import instead of typing them. See Bringing your existing records in.

docs.title: Editing and retiring
docs.text: Open a vehicle from the list to see its detail page, then Edit. Retiring a vehicle from service is a status change, not a deletion. Delete exists and cannot be undone, so it is the wrong tool for a truck you sold; change its status instead and keep its history on past incidents.

docs.title: The daily check
docs.text:
Checks are forms your crews fill in against a vehicle: the morning walk-around, a weekly SCBA check, a monthly ladder inspection. Open Apparatus & Equipment, then Checks.

The page has three tabs:

  • Overview shows the templates available and how the module is doing.
  • Submissions is the history: who checked what, when, and how it came out.
  • Schedule is the calendar of what is due.

Choose New Check to run one. Pick the template, pick the apparatus, and work down the form. If a check has items that can pass or fail, failing one records the problem against that vehicle so it is not lost when the crew changes over.

docs.title: Before your first check
docs.text: A check needs a template, and a template has to be published before anyone can fill it in. If the list is empty, that is why. See Forms, checks and inspections.

docs.title: What the numbers on the Overview mean
docs.text: The four cards count submissions: completed, pending, failed, and how many templates exist. They are a summary, not a filter, so clicking one does not narrow the list below. Use the Submissions tab to look through actual records.

docs.title: The status board
docs.text:
Status Board is what is happening right now: active calls, who is available, and which units are in service.

The board refreshes itself. Active incidents update about every half minute and the summary about every minute, and when the connection allows it, changes are pushed straight through rather than waited for.

Full roster & units at the bottom is collapsed until you open it, and only loads when you do. That is deliberate on a phone.

Two things chiefs ask about:

  • The board only shows calls that are ongoing and recent. An older call left open drops off. When that happens the page says so and offers a link to review the open incidents, so nothing is lost, but do not read an empty board as "nothing is open".
  • Responder positions come from the Rally app. Without Rally there are no pins. The map still works for the incident itself.

When you set a status that means you are responding or on scene, LadderOps records where you are at that moment. Your browser will ask permission the first time.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Messages is internal messaging: person to person, or a broadcast to the department.

Compose gives you two choices. A direct message goes to people you pick. A broadcast goes to everyone, or to particular stations if you name them.

Opening a message marks it read. There is no way to mark it unread again, so if you want to keep something in front of you, leave it unopened or send yourself a note.

The list does not poll. Use Refresh, or reopen the page, to check for new mail.

One caution worth knowing: if your account does not have access to messaging, the page currently shows an empty inbox rather than telling you so. An empty inbox on an account that should have messages is worth asking about rather than assuming nobody wrote.

docs.title: Department settings
docs.text: Settings is a grid of cards. Each opens one area. Most departments set these once during onboarding and rarely return.

docs.title: Department settings
docs.text:
One page, three groups, and one Save button at the bottom that saves all of it. There is no separate save per section.

Incident numbering controls what your incident numbers look like. The pattern accepts pieces you fill in: the year, the date, your department, and a sequence number that increases. A preview updates as you type, so you can see the shape before you commit to it.

Changing the pattern only affects new incidents. Nothing already recorded is renumbered, which is what you want; a report you filed under one number should keep it.

CAD integration is the switch that lets your dispatch center's email flow into LadderOps and create draft incidents. Leave it off until dispatch is actually sending to your LadderOps address, and read Sending your reports to NERIS and the dispatch section before turning it on. It does more than its label suggests, and we are fixing that wording.

Regional settings is your timezone, units, and a default map position. The map position is what the app centers on before it knows anything better, so set it to your district rather than leaving a default.

docs.title: Email notifications
docs.text:
This is outbound email: magic links, password resets, inspection reports being sent out. It is not about dispatch email coming in.

A route needs a name, an SMTP host and port, a username, a password, and a from address. Once saved, the password is never shown again; leaving it blank when editing keeps the one you have.

Send test email is worth using before you rely on it. Send one to yourself and confirm it arrives, rather than finding out when an inspection report does not reach a business owner.

docs.title: Narrative templates
docs.text:
A narrative template is not boilerplate text to copy. It shapes the two narrative boxes on the incident form: it gives each a prompt, and offers phrases you can click to insert.

Templates can be tied to an incident type, so a structure fire prompts for different things than a medical call, or left general.

Only the template name is required. A suggested minimum length is advice to the writer, not a rule; it will not stop a report being saved.

There is an option to draft one with AI, which costs about a cent and should be read before you keep it.

docs.title: Forms, checks and inspections
docs.text: Everything your crews used to do on a clipboard is a form: the daily truck check, an SCBA inventory, a business inspection, a training record. They all work the same way, so learning one teaches you the rest.

docs.title: Filling one in
docs.text:
Open Forms from the Records menu. The Fill a Form tab lists what is available; the buttons across the top filter by what the form is for.

Pick a form and work down it. Save Draft keeps your place without submitting. Submit sends it for approval.

If a form you expect is missing, one of two things is true: it is not active, or it has never been published. A template has to be published before anyone can fill it in, and until then the app will say so rather than let you start.

docs.title: Working without a signal
docs.text:
A form submitted with no connection is kept on the device and sent when you have one. You will see it confirm as saved offline, and a banner counts anything still waiting. It syncs on its own; Retry All is there if you want to push it.

This is deliberate. Filling in a check in a bay with no bars should not lose your work.

docs.title: Approving and rejecting
docs.text:
The Submissions tab is the history. While something is still awaiting a decision you can Approve it or Reject it, and rejecting asks for a reason. Once it is decided, those buttons go away.

Download PDF is available on submissions that are set up to produce one.

docs.title: Changing a form after it is submitted
docs.text: You can edit a submitted form, and LadderOps asks you why. That reason goes into the record, and the form goes back for approval again, because a changed record is a new thing to agree with. That is the point: correct the record, do not leave it wrong.

docs.title: Inspections
docs.text:
Prevention inspections are forms with a schedule attached. Open Prevention, then Inspections.

  • Overview shows your templates and counts.
  • Submissions is every inspection done.
  • Schedule is what is coming up.

Schedule Inspection books one against a business and a date. New Submission starts one now.

The counts on the Overview are a summary. Clicking one highlights it but does not filter the list; use the Submissions tab to search actual records.

Inspections you schedule against a business also show on that business's own record, under Businesses and occupancies.

docs.title: Telling us something is wrong
docs.text:
There is a Help button in the bottom right corner of every page. It opens two things: what has been written about the page you are on, and Report a problem.

Reporting from that button is the fastest way to get something fixed, and it is better than a phone call because of what it sends along with your message.

docs.title: Reading the manual
docs.text: The Help tab shows the chapters written about the page you are on. There is more in the full manual under Help in the menu, which you can search. Once you have opened it with a connection, it stays on the device and works without one.

docs.title: What to write
docs.text:
Two boxes, both short:

  • What went wrong, in a line. Plain words. "Truck check would not save" is perfect.
  • What you did, and what you expected. The steps you took, and what you thought would happen. "Hit Save on Engine 1's daily check and nothing happened. Tried twice."

You do not have to describe the technical side, and you should not try to. Do not include a patient's name or any of their details; the report is about the software, not the call.

docs.title: What gets sent with it
docs.text:
When you send the report, LadderOps attaches what an engineer would otherwise have to ask you for:

  • the page you were on
  • what the app asked the server for in the last few minutes, and what came back
  • any errors the app hit in the background
  • which version of LadderOps you were running

That is why a report filed from the screen where it happened is worth far more than one written up later from memory. If you hit something odd, stop and file it right then.

docs.title: What happens next
docs.text:
Your report goes straight to us with a status of open. We work the list and update the status as we go. If the fix needs something from you, we will get in touch through your usual channel.

For anything urgent, such as prod being down in the middle of a call, do not rely on the button. Phone.

docs.title: Your first week in LadderOps
docs.text: LadderOps replaces the paperwork side of running a department: the incident record that has to go to NERIS, the roster, the apparatus list, and the checks and inspections your crews already do on paper. This chapter is the short version of setting it up.

docs.title: The checklist does the setup for you
docs.text:
Open Getting started under Settings. It lists everything that has to exist before your first call can be reported, and it ticks each line off by itself as you go. Nothing here is busy work: the incident form pulls from these lists, so an empty roster means an incident you cannot staff and an empty aid list means typing NERIS IDs by hand on every call.

The lines you fill in are:

  • Create your department. Name, FDID, and department type. This is what NERIS matches your records against.
  • Stations added. One line per station, with its address.
  • Personnel added. Your roster, with each member's rank and status. You can add people one at a time or upload a spreadsheet from Import.
  • Apparatus added. Every engine, tanker, brush truck, and ambulance, with its call sign and how many it seats.
  • Aid partners added. The departments you run mutual or automatic aid with. See Recording mutual and automatic aid.

The lines above those, about modules, roles, and NERIS domains, are ours. They are already done before you sign in for the first time.

docs.title: Uploading a list instead of typing it
docs.text: If you already keep your roster or apparatus in a spreadsheet, use Import under Settings rather than retyping it. Upload the file as it is. LadderOps reads the column headings, shows you what it matched to what, and lets you correct anything it guessed wrong before a single row is saved. Nothing is written until you approve the preview.

docs.title: The dashboard
docs.text: The Dashboard is what your department looks like right now: calls this month and this year, how many are still drafts, what has gone to NERIS and what has not, plus anything overdue such as a check that was missed or a certification about to lapse. It is the page to open first thing in the morning and last thing before you go home.

docs.title: Working without a signal
docs.text: LadderOps is built for a truck bay with two bars. A report you start with no connection is kept on the device and sent as soon as you have one, so you can fill in a call standing at the scene and not lose it. You do not have to do anything to turn this on.

docs.title: When something looks wrong
docs.text: Every page has a Help button in the bottom right corner, with the manual for that page and a way to tell us something is wrong. Use it. See Telling us something is wrong.

docs.title: Bringing your existing records in
docs.text:
Most departments already keep a roster, an apparatus list, and hydrants somewhere: a spreadsheet, an old system's export, sometimes a printout. Import takes those as they are. You do not have to reformat anything first.

Open Import from Settings, or use the Import button on the page you are filling, which preselects what you are importing.

docs.title: What you can import
docs.text:
Personnel, apparatus, units, stations, locations, occupancies, certification types, personnel certifications, water sources, and Quartermaster assets.

Files can be CSV, Excel, PDF, images, GeoJSON, JSON or a zip, up to 25 MB.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Upload. Choose what you are importing and pick the file.
  2. Read. LadderOps reads the file and works out which of your columns means what. It usually takes ten to thirty seconds, and it will tell you where it is less sure.
  3. Review. Every row is shown before anything is saved, marked as ready, an update to an existing record, skipped, a warning, needing a decision, or an error. Fix what you want to fix, and where a field needs a value your department has not set up yet, you can create it right there.
  4. Import. Only then is anything written.

Nothing is saved until you press the import button. You can back out at any point before that.

docs.title: Partial imports are normal
docs.text: If some rows have errors and others are fine, the good rows import and the problem rows stay behind for a second pass. You do not have to fix a whole file to make progress on it, and you do not have to hunt for which rows went in: the result tells you how many were created, updated and skipped.

docs.title: If the file mentions a department you do not have
docs.text: Roster exports often carry a department identifier from an old system. If it does not match yours, LadderOps offers to treat it as your department, or to create the department, and then rechecks every row without you uploading again.

docs.title: Undoing
docs.text: Undo import removes everything a single import created. It is meant for the "that was the wrong file" case, and it works for a period after the import rather than forever. Check the result screen at the time rather than relying on it days later.

docs.title: Businesses, occupancies and pre-plans
docs.text: These three pages answer one question: what do we already know about this address before we get there.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text:
A location is an address. It is the thing everything else attaches to, so it comes first.

Open Locations from Prevention and choose New Location. Nothing is strictly required, but an address is the point of the record.

Two things worth knowing about coordinates:

  • If you type an address, LadderOps looks it up and sets the coordinates for you. That happens every time you change the address fields, and it replaces what was there. If the lookup finds nothing, it clears the coordinates rather than leaving a stale pin.
  • If you set the position with Pick on Map, or type coordinates yourself, LadderOps treats them as deliberate and stops overwriting them.

So: place the pin by hand when the address is not one a map service will find, which for rural districts is often.

docs.title: Occupancies
docs.text:
An occupancy is a business or building you inspect. Open Occupancies from Prevention.

Only the business name is required. Everything else, address included, is optional, so you can get a list down quickly and fill in detail later.

A business record has tabs for its inspections, the incidents you have run there, cautions, and its pre-plan. Cautions are the things a crew needs shouted at them on the way: dogs, solar, oxygen, a floor that is not safe. Only currently active cautions show, so a caution can exist and not appear if it has been ended.

The Knox box details on a business are stored on the underlying location, which is why they follow the address rather than the tenant.

docs.title: Pre-plans
docs.text:
A pre-plan is what you want the first-arriving officer to have read. Open Pre-Plans, choose New Pre-Plan, and pick the location.

One pre-plan per location. If someone already made one, LadderOps will tell you rather than create a second.

The building information at the top, construction, stories, sprinklers, Knox box, alarm and hazards, is read only in the pre-plan. It comes from the location record and is edited there. This is the single most common question about this page: if the construction type is wrong, fix it on the location.

Contacts and hazmat units can only be added after the plan is saved once.

Publish makes a plan available to crews. That matters more than it sounds: only published plans are kept on the device for offline use. A draft is not there when you have no signal, which is exactly when you want it. Publish anything you would want on a call.

docs.title: Your roster and certifications
docs.text: Everyone who responds needs a record, because incidents are staffed from the roster and certifications are tracked against it.

docs.title: Adding people
docs.text:
Open Personnel from the menu. The Roster tab lists everyone. Choose New Personnel.

Required: organization, first name, last name, rank, and status. Station and unit assignments are optional and are saved separately after the person is created, so if something goes wrong at that step the person still exists and you can set the assignment from their record.

For a whole roster at once, use Import rather than typing. See Bringing your existing records in.

docs.title: The four tabs
docs.text:
• Roster is your people.
  • Certifications here is the catalog of certification types your department tracks: Firefighter I, EMT-Basic, Driver Operator. It is the list of what exists, not who holds what.
  • Assignments shows who is attached to which station and unit.
  • Response activity is drawn from the Rally app. If your department does not use Rally, this stays empty. Nothing here is typed in by hand; it is a record of who actually responded.

docs.title: Who holds what
docs.text:
Individual certifications are recorded on a person's own record, under their Certifications tab. That is where you add "this firefighter holds EMT-Basic, expiring on this date".

To see the whole department at once, open Certifications from the menu. That page is the expiration dashboard, not the catalog. It shows four counts across your whole roster: active, expiring in 30 days, expiring in 90 days, and expired.

Three of those cards filter the list when you click them. The 90 day card is a count only. Click an active filter again to clear it.

The list is always sorted the same way, worst first: expired, then whatever expires soonest. That ordering is deliberate and is not adjustable, because the whole point of the page is what needs attention first.

docs.title: Removing someone
docs.text: There is no delete button on a person's own record. To remove someone, select them on the Roster list and use the bulk action. Most of the time the right answer is a status change rather than a deletion, so their name stays correct on the incidents they ran.

docs.title: Reporting a call
docs.text: Every call your department runs becomes one incident record, and that record is what NERIS receives. This is the flow from the tones dropping to a submitted report.

docs.title: Start the report
docs.text:
From Incidents, choose New incident. You need three things before the form will let you go on: when the call came in, where it was, and what type of call it was. Everything else can be filled in later.

The address box searches as you type and drops a pin on the map. If the address does not come up, place the pin by hand; the coordinates are what NERIS wants, and the street address is for your own records.

docs.title: Fill in the rest as you learn it
docs.text:
The form is grouped into sections down the page, and you can work them in any order:

  • Response and operations. Which units went, who was on them, and the times: dispatched, en route, on scene, cleared. If your dispatch center emails your calls to LadderOps, most of these times are already filled in.
  • Fire, EMS, hazmat, or wildland detail. Only the sections that match your call type appear. A structure fire asks about the building and what burned; a medical call asks about the patient's care, not their name.
  • Aid. Departments that helped you or that you helped. See Recording mutual and automatic aid.
  • Narrative. What happened, in your own words. If your department uses narrative templates, pick one and it fills in the skeleton for you.

Your work is saved as you go. If you close the app or lose signal in the middle, the draft is still there when you come back.

docs.title: Check it before it goes anywhere
docs.text:
In the last section, choose Validate Report. LadderOps runs your report against the NERIS rules and tells you how many passed, then lists anything it found:

  • Errors have to be fixed. NERIS will not accept the record with them.
  • Warnings are worth a second look but do not stop you. An alarm time earlier than the time the call was reported, for example, is unusual but perfectly possible, so LadderOps flags it rather than blocking it.

Each finding names the field it came from, so you can click it and land on the box to fix.

docs.title: Submit it
docs.text: Once validation is clean, Submit to NERIS appears. After it goes, the record shows the NERIS status and a link to the NERIS portal. See Sending your reports to NERIS for what those statuses mean.

docs.title: Changing a report after it is submitted
docs.text: You can still open a submitted incident and edit it. LadderOps records who changed what and when, so the correction is traceable. That is the point: fix the record rather than leaving it wrong.

docs.title: Reports and looking back
docs.text: Reports under Records answers the questions you get asked once a year and cannot remember: how many calls, what kind, who turned out, how fast.

docs.title: The filter bar
docs.text: Everything on the page obeys the filters at the top. The date range defaults to the last 30 days, and there are presets up to all time. Change it once and every tab follows.

docs.title: The tabs
docs.text:
• Overview is the headline: call volume and how it is trending.
  • By Type breaks calls down by what they were.
  • Responders is who turned out.
  • Response is timing.
  • Explorer is the raw list, for when you want to see the calls themselves rather than a chart.

docs.title: Aid, and why your numbers can look wrong
docs.text:
This is the part that surprises people.

Calls you assisted another department on are filed by that department, not by you. They are not in your own records, so by default they are not in your numbers. There is a switch, include other departments' records, that pulls in calls where NERIS shows you were involved.

Two things about it:

  • It is off by default, so your default numbers are your own calls only.
  • It affects the summary, the trend, the breakdown by type and by town. It does not change Explorer, Responders or Response.

There is also a separate filter for the direction of aid, given or received. That is a different question from whether to include the other department's records at all, and the page explains which is which as you use it.

If your mutual aid numbers look too low, that switch is almost always the reason.

docs.title: Exporting
docs.text:
Export on the Explorer tab produces a spreadsheet of the rows you are looking at. On the chart tabs it produces a PDF of that section.

The Responders tab has no export today. The button is there and does nothing, which is a known gap rather than something you are doing wrong.

docs.title: Scheduling and shift signups
docs.text: Scheduling covers two different things that live on one page, and telling them apart makes the page much easier to use.

docs.title: One-off shifts: the week board
docs.text:
The Week board is the calendar. A shift here is a specific block of time with people assigned to it: a standby for a parade, an extra crew for a storm, a duty crew on Saturday.

New shift creates one. Name, organization, start and end are required, and the end has to be after the start. Assign people from your roster.

On duty now, at the top, always shows who is covering at this moment. That is the answer to the question the page gets opened for most.

docs.title: Recurring coverage: roster and signups
docs.text:
The Roster & signups tab is the other model: A, B and C style platoon patterns that repeat, where people sign up for slots and swap between themselves rather than being assigned each time.

Members sign up for open slots and can propose trades. An officer approves or denies both.

If this tab says no recurring configurations are set up, the platoon patterns have not been created yet. That is an administrative step and it is separate from creating a shift on the week board.

docs.title: Who can approve
docs.text: Approving and denying signups and trades is limited to chiefs and administrators. Everyone else can sign up and propose a trade, and will not see the approve and deny buttons.

docs.title: A note on refreshing
docs.text: The page does not update itself. If you are working an approval queue alongside someone else, reload before you assume you are looking at the current state.

docs.title: Sending your reports to NERIS
docs.text: NERIS is the national incident reporting system that replaced NFIRS. Your department reports into it directly from LadderOps, so there is no export file to download and no second website to key your calls into.

docs.title: Connect your department once
docs.text:
You need two things from FSRI, who run NERIS: a client ID and a client secret for your department. They are issued to your department, not to a person, and they arrive when your NERIS enrollment is approved.

Open NERIS Integration under Settings, paste both in, and save. The secret is stored encrypted and is never shown again after you save it; if it is ever lost, FSRI issue a new one rather than telling you the old one.

Then choose Test Connection. A good result means LadderOps reached NERIS as your department and NERIS recognized the credentials. Do this before your first real call rather than finding out at two in the morning.

docs.title: What the statuses mean
docs.text:
After a report is submitted, its NERIS status appears on the incident. LadderOps rechecks every submitted report once a day, so a status that changes on the NERIS side shows up here without you doing anything.

  • Submitted. NERIS has the record.
  • Pending approval. NERIS is holding it for review. This is normal and needs nothing from you.
  • Pending incident data. NERIS is waiting on something the record did not carry.
  • Approved. Done. The call is on the national record.
  • Rejected. NERIS refused the record. Open the incident, fix what it names, and submit again.
  • Failed. The submission itself did not go through, usually a connection problem rather than anything wrong with your report. Try again.

If a status has never been checked, the incident shows nothing rather than guessing.

docs.title: If you are not connected yet
docs.text: Everything else in LadderOps works without NERIS. You can report calls, run checks and inspections, and keep your roster. Reports pile up as ready to submit, and once your credentials are in they can be sent. Nothing is lost by starting before your enrollment comes through.

docs.title: Getting your credentials
docs.text: If you do not have a client ID and secret yet, your NERIS enrollment is not finished. That is between your department and FSRI, at neris.fsri.org. We can walk you through it; use Report a problem and say so.

docs.title: Hydrants and water supply
docs.text: Water Supply under Prevention is every hydrant, draft site, cistern and dry hydrant you can pull from, with the detail a driver needs at three in the morning.

docs.title: Adding sources
docs.text:
New Water Source adds one. The List and Map buttons switch how you look at them.

Coordinates work differently here from the rest of LadderOps: there is no address lookup. Latitude and longitude are shown but not typed. You set a position with Pick on map, or move one with Reposition on map. For rural water sources that is usually right anyway, since a draft site rarely has a street address that a map service would find.

If your county publishes hydrants as a map layer, Sync pulls them in rather than making you type them. You need the feature layer address; the access token, if the layer needs one, is stored and never shown again. A sync runs in the background, and the page watches it for about half a minute before it stops watching. If it is still going, come back and use Refresh status.

docs.title: Compliance
docs.text: Compliance is the NFPA 291 side: which hydrants are due an inspection or a flow test, and which are overdue. Switch between overdue and due soon, and download the list as a spreadsheet if you work from paper.

docs.title: One limit worth knowing
docs.text: The map view loads up to one hundred sources at a time. If your department has more than that, the map is not showing all of them. The list view is not affected and will page through everything. If you have just imported a county hydrant layer, work from the list until this is fixed.
